Oil: two tankers hit near Hormuz, a Saudi refinery struck in Jazan, Brent climbs to $96.57 ahead of Sunday's OPEC+ meeting

On Thursday, November 26, Brent, Europe's benchmark crude, ended at $96.57 a barrel, up $1.96, its highest level since November 6. The causes: two tankers hit by mines near the Omani port of Khasab, according to Iran, and a deadly strike on Saudi Arabia's Jazan refinery [1][2][3].

The Revolutionary Guards, Iran's ideological army, say two tankers struck mines north of Khasab, in Oman, while trying to cross the Strait of Hormuz. This account has not been independently confirmed [1].

The same day, a projectile hit Aramco's refinery in Jazan, in southwestern Saudi Arabia. According to the Saudi Energy Ministry, a Nepalese worker was killed, several people were injured and part of the facilities was shut down for a time; the fire was brought under control [3].
Riyadh did not name the perpetrator, but the Saudi-led coalition blames Yemen's Houthi rebels, who are allied with Iran. The refinery can process up to 400,000 barrels a day [3].
Brent gained 1.2% on Thursday. US crude, WTI, had no closing price, as Wall Street was closed for Thanksgiving: it was trading at $84.84 in early afternoon in New York [1].
On Friday morning, Brent was down 38 cents at $96.19 at 1:40 a.m. GMT [2]. It is heading for its first weekly gain in four weeks, of about 4.5%, but is still down nearly 20% for the month [2][4].
A barrel for immediate delivery costs nearly $4 more than deliveries further out, a sign that available oil is in short supply [2].

On Sunday, November 29, ministers from OPEC+, the alliance of major producing countries led by Saudi Arabia and Russia, are due to set their quotas for 2027. According to two sources close to the talks, they are expected to keep current targets at least until the end of March 2027 [5].
Key takeaway: after three weeks of decline, oil is rising again because the war now affects both the Gulf's shipping routes and Saudi refineries [2][4].

For Rory Johnston of the firm Commodity Context, Brent was “oversold” below $90: there is a “known and acute” risk to about 15% of global supply [1]. Analysts at ANZ bank, Brian Martin and Daniel Hynes, believe the barrel could go back above $100 even without a new major escalation, provided physical deliveries tighten [2].

OPEC+ itself is divided. Iraq disputes a first estimate that puts its production capacity at 4.9 million barrels a day, and Kazakhstan is also challenging its own. Yet these capacities are to serve as the basis for the 2027 quotas: Russian Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak promises to finish the assessment by the end of the year [5].
And demand fell in 2026, with no full recovery expected in 2027, according to the ICIS agency [6].

The price of a barrel shows up a few weeks later at the pump and in the price of heating oil, just as winter begins. If Brent goes back above $100, filling your tank and heating your home could cost more in December.

news.2026-11-27-policiers-etudiants-mobi: Paris, France
France
Thursday of anger: police officers rally outside their stations over their risk bonus, students take to the streets again

On Thursday, November 26, police officers gathered outside police stations across France to demand that their risk bonus be raised to 35% of their base salary [1][3]. The same day, a few thousand students marched, mainly in Paris, for more university places [7][8].

The Alliance union issued the call, joined by Unsa Police and Un1té; rallies were planned from noon “outside every police station in France” [2][4]. Night-shift officers started at midnight, and slowdowns were reported at the borders [5].

At the heart of the dispute: the special police duties allowance (ISSP), the risk bonus, which has not been raised since 2019 [3]. On November 13, Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez proposed raising it from 28.5% to 33.5% over three years, until 2029, with a first step in April 2027 [3].
Alliance calls these responses “unacceptable” and demands 35% right away. “It's 35% or nothing,” sums up its general secretary, Fabien Vanhemelryck [3].

In Rennes, the Unité union is also calling for higher pay for assistant police officers and warning about officers' exhaustion and mental health [6]. Unsa says the actions are not disrupting service [5].

On the student side, the Paris march set off at 2 p.m. from Bastille toward the Panthéon, on a route authorized by the police prefecture; franceinfo put the turnout at about 2,000 people, and it ended peacefully [7].

The number of blockades at high schools and universities is falling, but new demonstrations are planned for Saturday [8]. On November 10, Lecornu promised 5,000 more places in undergraduate programs, including 4,000 in IUTs (university technology institutes), on top of the 15,000 already announced [9][10]. Student organizations are asking for 250,000 [9].
Key takeaway: the government, which is looking for savings to cut the deficit, is facing spending demands from several sides at once, such as those of the police and the students [3][9].

For the police, the gap looks small, 33.5% versus 35%, but it is mainly about timing: right away rather than in three steps through 2029 [3]. The unions warn that the movement could grow if negotiations fail [1].

Among young people, the movement has been going on since mid-September: university students have joined high school students, with rallies and blockades [9]. It is losing steam, but the government's promises remain very far from the demands [8][9].

If the police bonus goes up, it's one more public expense in an already strained budget. And if you're a student or the parent of a future high school graduate, the number of undergraduate places directly determines the chances of getting into the program you want next year.

New Zealand: special votes cost Luxon his majority, the small Opportunity party becomes kingmaker and a new election is no longer ruled out

The official results of New Zealand's general election, released on Friday, November 27, strip Prime Minister Christopher Luxon's right-wing coalition of its majority: 65 seats out of 130, one short of the 66 needed. The Opportunity party and its 7 MPs now hold the key to the next government [1][3][4].

“Special” votes (New Zealanders abroad, late-registered voters, etc.), counted after election night, changed everything: 484,865 ballots, far more than the 399,365 estimated by the Electoral Commission [1].

Final result: the National Party (right) 40 seats, Labour (left) 36, the Greens 17, ACT 13, NZ First 12, Opportunity 7 and Te Pāti Māori 5 [1][2][3]. The National Party loses two seats compared with election night, while Labour and the Greens gain one each [3].

Three electorates changed hands [7]. In Wairarapa, Labour's Kieran McAnulty finished 81 votes ahead of National's Mike Butterick, who had led by 139 votes on election night [1]. In Hamilton East, Labour's Georgie Dansey won by 173 votes, after National's Ryan Hamilton had been 456 votes ahead [1].

Christopher Luxon, who had ruled out an alliance with Opportunity at least 19 times during the campaign, is changing his tune: “Kiwis won't thank us for going back to the polls,” he said, announcing that “formal negotiations will begin” with the party [5][6].

Opportunity leader Qiulae Wong says she is ready to talk to both sides [6]. She has set five “non-negotiable” conditions, including an immediate phase-out of bottom trawling and lobbying reform [8], and demands that Winston Peters, leader of NZ First, not remain foreign minister [8].
Labour's Chris Hipkins rules out a “grand coalition” with the National Party and will not call Christopher Luxon to concede defeat [4].
Key takeaway: New Zealand is left with a hung Parliament. If the outgoing coalition and Opportunity fail to reach an agreement, a new election becomes possible [1][4].
The paradox: Labour came first in the vote (29.88% versus 28.35%), but the National Party keeps the most seats (40 versus 36), because it won more electorates [10][2].

Opportunity is also calling for the competition authority (the Commerce Commission) to be able to investigate companies that abuse their position and even force them to break up [9]. Such a deal would therefore weigh on economic policy, not just on the political balance.
The numbers could still change: the National Party is expected to request a recount in Wairarapa, with requests possible until December 3 [2][3].

No direct effect on your daily life. But it's a textbook case of proportional representation, often debated in France: a party with 7 MPs can decide who governs and impose its priorities, such as ending bottom trawling or tighter oversight of competition [8][9]. Worth following if you're interested in how coalitions are formed.

Argentina
Argentina: the central bank will no longer be allowed to lend to the state, Congress passes Milei's reform and the Senate suspends the 2027 primaries

During the “super Thursday” of November 26 in Argentina's Congress, deputies gave final approval to the central bank reform sought by Javier Milei, by 141 votes with none against, and the Senate voted to suspend the 2027 primaries, by 43 votes to 29. The 2027 budget was still being debated overnight [1][2][4].
Central bank: the Chamber of Deputies accepted the Senate's amendments, with 141 votes in favor, none against and 99 abstentions [1][4]. The bill now goes to the presidency to be signed into law [1].
Its new main goal: preserving the value of the peso. Employment, growth and social equity are removed from its mandate [3][4].

It will no longer be able to lend to the state, the provinces or municipalities, or to buy government debt securities when they are issued. “Temporary advances,” direct loans to the Treasury, are abolished [3][4].
Senators softened one point: appointing or dismissing its leaders will require an absolute majority of the Senate, 37 votes, rather than the two-thirds Milei wanted [1][4].

Primaries: the electoral reform passed by the Senate suspends for 2027 the mandatory primaries, known as PASO, in which all voters choose among each party's candidates [2][5]. Each party will choose according to its own rules, with a single list per category [5].

The bill also cuts public funding for parties, scraps the mandatory presidential debate and includes “Ficha Limpia,” a mechanism designed to bar candidates convicted of corruption [2][5][7]. It was backed by La Libertad Avanza, Milei's party, the UCR Radicals, PRO and Provincias Unidas, while the Peronists opposed it [6][7].
2027 budget: deputies opened the session at 12:19 p.m. with 130 members present [8]. The government was counting on about 126 votes and a vote around midnight [10][11].

Key takeaway: Milei is enshrining a central promise in law, no longer creating money to finance state deficits. The mechanism is simple: when the central bank lends to the Treasury, it creates pesos, and too many pesos in circulation push prices up [3][4].
The electoral reform still has to go through the Chamber of Deputies, during extraordinary sessions; if deputies amend it, it will go back to the Senate [5][6].

On the budget, the most contested point is funding for universities: the bill grants them 7.3 trillion pesos, versus the 11 trillion demanded by the National Interuniversity Council [9]. In committee, on November 17, the bill had gathered only 27 signatures out of 48, after concessions on aid for people with disabilities and the auto industry [12].
Congress has until December 31. Without a vote, the government would have to roll over the 2026 budget to govern next year [12].

A central bank that can no longer finance the state is the rule that already applies to the ECB in the eurozone. If you travel to or invest in Argentina, it's a bet on a more stable peso in the future.

Asian stock markets: Seoul rebounds again on Friday but ends November down 16%, Taiwan down 15%

On Friday, November 27, Asian stock markets ended the week higher, lifted by chipmakers: Seoul gained about 2%, Tokyo 0.7%. But November's tally remains heavy: −16% for South Korea, −15% for Taiwan, −8.4% for Japan's Nikkei [1][2].

MSCI's index of Asia-Pacific shares outside Japan gained 0.5% on Friday and 1.9% for the week, but is still down 8.2% in November [1]. Tokyo's Nikkei rose 0.7% [1][4], or 2.7% for the week, after an 8.4% drop for the month [1].

In Seoul, the Kospi gained about 2% according to Reuters [1], 3% according to Bloomberg [2]. Samsung Electronics rose 3.6% and SK Hynix 2.9% [2]. In Taipei, the index advanced 0.8%, TSMC 1.2% and Foxconn 1.3% [2].

Around 2:30 a.m. GMT, Hong Kong's Hang Seng was up 0.6% at 22,366 points, and the Shanghai index 0.3%, according to AFP [3]. In Tokyo, memory chipmaker Kioxia drew buyers after a week of heavy selling [3].

On November 24, the Taiwan stock market jumped 8.99%, its biggest gain in points in its history [7]. The next day, it fell 4.80% [8], and Seoul 6.16%, to 4,697.51 points, with −9.87% for Samsung and −11.05% for SK Hynix [6].

Analysts quoted by AFP expect more turbulence, as investors wonder whether artificial intelligence will really pay off [3]. MSCI's emerging markets index is heading for its third straight monthly decline [2].

The dollar, for its part, is heading for a third month of gains, +1.8% in November against major currencies [1]. In Tokyo, inflation excluding fresh food reached 2.9% year on year in November, the highest in 16 months, versus 3% expected [5].

Key takeaway: South Korea and Taiwan, the world's chip champions, have become the stock markets most exposed to doubts about AI. When those doubts grow, they fall harder than the others; when they recede, they also rebound harder [2][6].

Two forces are combining. On one hand, investors wonder whether the billions spent on AI will earn enough to justify chipmakers' share prices [3]. On the other, the strong dollar and the prospect of higher interest rates in the United States make US investments more attractive [1].

In Japan, the Bank of Japan has a decision to make: Tokyo's inflation argues for a rate hike as early as December, which most economists polled by Reuters expect [5]. Board member Naoki Tamura called on Thursday for a “swift” response to signs of prices getting out of hand [5]. But one economist warns that it could hold off if market instability persists [5].

If you hold a “global equities” or “emerging markets” fund in your stock savings plan (PEA) or life insurance policy, Samsung, SK Hynix and TSMC carry a lot of weight in it: November pulled it down. Their stock market troubles won't immediately change the price of your phone or computer.

How it works: why a stock market can lose 16% in a month and rebound 9% in a day

A stock market dominated by a few giants follows their fortunes. When investors have doubts about AI chips, they sell Samsung and SK Hynix, and Seoul's entire index plunges: on November 25, −9.87% and −11.05% for these two groups, −6.16% for the Kospi [6]. Many have also bought on credit: when the price falls, their bank asks them to put up more money, otherwise it sells their shares, which speeds up the fall. Conversely, at the slightest good news, sellers rush to buy back and the market soars, like Taiwan on November 24 (+8.99%) [7]. Hence this roller coaster.

news.2026-11-27-canada-yukon-centrales-w: Canada: touring the Far North, Carney designates two new power plants in Whitehorse, Yukon, as being in the “national interest”

On Thursday, November 26, in Whitehorse, Prime Minister Mark Carney referred the Whitehorse Power Centres project to the Major Projects Office, alongside Yukon Premier Currie Dixon. This federal office is designed to speed up projects deemed to be in the national interest [1][2].
The project first calls for two new thermal power plants, a substation and transmission lines in Whitehorse [1].
A first phase is to add 15 megawatts by 2027, then about 150 megawatts with the following phases [2].
The Major Projects Office will help Yukon assess the grid upgrades needed and will study Indigenous equity participation [2][3].
Earlier on Thursday, Mark Carney was campaigning in Yorkton and then met Saskatchewan Premier Scott Moe in Regina, ahead of six by-elections on December 7 [4].

Key takeaway: Ottawa wants to prove it can build quickly in the North, where electricity is scarce, and is placing the project within a broader plan that includes connecting Yukon's grid to British Columbia [1].
On Friday the 27th, Mark Carney is due to announce in Yellowknife, with Northwest Territories Premier R.J. Simpson, a “major new initiative” to “connect and transform Canada's North” [5].
Canada's Far North is rich in minerals that Europe needs for batteries and industry, but electricity is needed to extract them: these projects also affect our supplies.
